---
title: "Units of analysis"
toc: true
---

## Why units matter
Criminology claims look different depending on whether you study:
- **persons**, **places**, **networks**, **institutions**, or **time**.

A good academic note states its unit explicitly.

---

## Person-level (micro)
Typical questions:
- Why do some individuals offend repeatedly?
- What predicts onset/desistance?

Model primitives:
- types, constraints, dynamic states (employment, stigma), discounting/self-control.

Pitfall:
- selection into arrest/conviction is not identical to selection into offending.

---

## Place-level (spatial)
Typical questions:
- Why do hotspots exist?
- Do interventions displace crime?

Model primitives:
- opportunity/guardianship, spatial choice, congestion, displacement.

Pitfall:
- shifting crime across blocks can look like “success” locally but not globally.

---

## Network-level (social)
Typical questions:
- Why co-offending clusters?
- How do tactics diffuse?

Model primitives:
- strategic complements, learning, partner choice, trust/betrayal, diffusion.

Pitfall:
- peer effects vs sorting (who befriends whom) are easy to confuse empirically.

---

## Institutional level (police/courts/corrections)
Typical questions:
- How do agencies allocate scarce resources?
- How do discretion and incentives shape outcomes?

Model primitives:
- objectives, constraints, information, capacity, performance measures.

Pitfall:
- “crime falls after more policing” can reflect recording/classification changes too.

---

## Time / dynamics
Typical questions:
- When does policy have short-run vs long-run effects?
- How do offenders adapt?

Model primitives:
- dynamic games, Markov states, learning, reputation, equilibrium adjustment.

Pitfall:
- ignoring adaptation can overstate policy impact.

---

## Practical rule
If your theory prediction is about **behavior**, say so.  
If your prediction is about **recorded outcomes**, say which stage (reporting, recording, clearance, conviction) is affected.
